content: In settings with high malaria transmission, the likelihood of patients with high parasitemia developing severe malaria is reduced. However, uncomplicated hyperparasitemia is still associated with a significantly elevated risk of treatment failure. Patients with parasitemia levels between 4% and 10%, even in the absence of severe symptoms, require close monitoring and, if possible, hospital admission due to their high rates of treatment failure. Non-immune individuals, such as travelers or those in low-transmission areas, with parasitemia levels exceeding 2% are at increased risk and also require careful attention. Parasitemia levels above 10% are universally considered indicative of severe malaria. Making general treatment recommendations for uncomplicated hyperparasitemia is challenging for several reasons. Accurate quantitative parasite counts are necessary to identify these patients, as semi-quantitative thick film counts or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are insufficient. The risks of severe malaria and treatment failure vary significantly, and there is limited data on therapeutic responses in uncomplicated hyperparasitemia. Ensuring the absorption of the first dose of artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is critical to prevent progression to severe malaria. Atovaquone-proguanil alone should not be used for travelers presenting with uncomplicated hyperparasitemia. Longer treatment courses, such as extended ACT regimens or preceding the standard 3-day ACT regimen with parenteral or oral artesunate, have shown greater efficacy. Plasmodium vivax accounts for approximately half of all malaria cases outside Africa and is prevalent in regions such as the Middle East, Asia, the Western Pacific, and Central and South America. In Africa, it is less common due to the high prevalence of the Duffy-negative phenotype, particularly in West Africa, although cases have been reported in Mauritania and Mali. In areas where P. vivax is prevalent, malaria transmission rates are generally low, except on the island of New Guinea. Populations in these regions develop only partial immunity, leaving individuals of all ages at risk for P. vivax malaria. Where both P. falciparum and P. vivax coexist, P. vivax incidence tends to peak at a younger age due to frequent relapses following each inoculation. Other human malaria species, such as P. malariae and P. ovale (which consists of two sympatric species), are less common. P. knowlesi, a simian parasite, occasionally causes malaria in or near forested areas of Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent. In parts of Borneo, P. knowlesi is the predominant cause of human malaria and a significant cause of severe malaria. Of the six Plasmodium species affecting humans, only P. vivax and the two P. ovale species form hypnozoites, dormant liver stages that can cause relapses weeks to years after the initial infection. P. vivax preferentially invades reticulocytes, and repeated infections can lead to chronic anemia, which may be debilitating and life-threatening, particularly in young children. Recurrent vivax malaria poses a significant barrier to human and economic development in affected populations. In areas where P. falciparum and P. vivax coexist, intensive malaria control efforts often have a greater impact on P. falciparum, as P. vivax is more resilient to interventions. Although P. vivax has historically been considered a benign form of malaria, it can sometimes cause severe disease, with anemia being the primary complication in young children. In regions with intense malaria transmission, such as Papua Province in Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, P. vivax is a major cause of malaria-related morbidity and mortality, particularly in young infants and children. Occasionally, older patients may develop severe organ involvement similar to that seen in severe P. falciparum malaria. During pregnancy, P. vivax infection increases the risk of miscarriage and reduces birth weight. In primigravidae, the reduction in birth weight is approximately two-thirds of that associated with P. falciparum, and this effect increases with successive pregnancies. P. knowlesi is a zoonotic parasite that primarily infects longand pig-tailed macaques. It has a daily asexual replication cycle, leading to rapid parasite multiplication and high parasitemia levels. P. knowlesi can cause fulminant disease resembling severe falciparum malaria, except for coma, which does not occur. Co-infection with other Plasmodium species is common. Diagnosis of P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. malariae malaria is based on microscopy. P. knowlesi is often misdiagnosed under the microscope due to its young ring forms resembling those of P. falciparum and its late trophozoites resembling those of P. malariae. Parasite development in P. knowlesi is asynchronous. RDTs for P. vivax malaria are available but are relatively insensitive for detecting P. malariae and P. ovale parasitemia. RDTs for human Plasmodium species show poor sensitivity for P. knowlesi infections in humans with low parasitemia. The treatment of vivax malaria aims to achieve two objectives: curing the acute blood-stage infection and clearing hypnozoites from the liver to prevent future relapses, a process known as radical cure. In areas with chloroquine-sensitive P. vivax, oral chloroquine at a total dose of 25 mg base/kg body weight is effective and well-tolerated. Lower doses are not recommended, as they promote resistance. Chloroquine is administered as an initial dose of 10 mg base/kg body weight, followed by 10 mg/kg on the second day and 5 mg/kg on the third day. Residual chloroquine suppresses the first relapse of tropical P. vivax, which typically emerges about three weeks after the onset of the primary illness. Without radical curative treatment with primaquine, relapses begin to occur 5–7 weeks after treatment. ACTs are effective against all malaria infections, with the exception of artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP), where resistance significantly compromises efficacy. While good efficacy of artesunate + SP has been reported in some studies, such as in Afghanistan, resistance to SP in P. vivax has emerged more rapidly than in P. falciparum in several regions, including Southeast Asia. The initial response to all ACTs in vivax malaria is rapid, reflecting the high sensitivity to artemisinin derivatives. However, relapses commonly follow unless primaquine is administered. The recurrence patterns differ based on the elimination kinetics of the partner drugs. For example, recurrences occur earlier after artemether-lumefantrine than after dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine or artesunate-mefloquine, as lumefantrine is eliminated more rapidly than mefloquine or piperaquine. In areas with chloroquine-resistant P. vivax, ACTs containing piperaquine, mefloquine, or lumefantrine are the recommended treatments, although artesunate + amodiaquine may also be effective in some regions. Resistance of P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi to antimalarial drugs is not well-characterized, but these species are generally considered sensitive to chloroquine. Mixed malaria infections are common in endemic areas and are best detected using nucleic acid-based amplification techniques, such as PCR, as routine microscopy may underestimate their prevalence. ACTs are effective against all malaria species and are the treatment of choice for mixed infections.
